newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania c.bank chief urges faster economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Romania c.bank chief urges faster economic reforms.

text.p: Romania's central bank chief on Thursday urged swift economic reform to underpin tighter monetary policies coupled with planned liberalisation moves, as the country resumed loan talks with the IMF and World Bank.

"We need a credible, strong programme, including tough reforms," central bank governor Mugur Isarescu told Reuters. "If we move fast, we should have the guidelines, if not the bulk of the programme ready within three weeks."

Romania's centrist ruling coalition, which toppled ex-communists in last November's elections, is working on a reform package aimed at restoring economic stability and accelerating structural reforms.

Isarescu said that reforms needed to be made soon to back up monetary policy. "Tight monetary policies have an optimal life span of nine to 15 months. If they are not backed by structural reforms, beyond that they become unsustainable," he said.
On Thursday Romanian officials were due to resume loan negotiations with the International Monetary Fund in Bucharest, in parallel with continuing talks with the World Bank.
Both international lenders withheld loan tranches for Romania last year due to slow reforms and overspending by the former ruling leftists in an electoral year.
The central bank is pushing on with a drive to tighten monetary policies, lifting its key interest rates to restore confidence in the sagging leu.
But Isarescu urged privatisation and restructuring of industries using large amounts of energy, which are contributing to Romania's bulging deficits.
Faster restructuring would boost efforts to free the foreign exchange market within the next two months, "in a country whose economy depends to a large extent on energy imports", he said.
Romania is faced with large budget and trade deficits, while debts piled up by big state-owned transport, energy and oil distribution companies total $629 million.
The former leftist administration's attempts to keep the leu currency overvalued reignited inflation, which had been slashed to 27.8 percent in 1995 from about 300 in 1993.

Year-on-year inflation which rose to 47.4 percent last November -- exceeding the 20 percent target agreed with the Fund -- is expected to climb again after the new cabinet doubled fuel prices this month to bring them up to world levels.
Isarescu declined to give a forecast for 1997 inflation but linked its evolution with the timing of reforms.
"A forecast for 1997 depends on three factors," he said, listing further price corrections for electricity, heating and staples, including meat, milk and bread.
"The government inclines to take a coherent approach, rather than piecemeal price adjustments. In our opinion, a coherent and comprehensive approach is the best."
But he said two factors could weigh upon the fragile balance -- trade unionism and "public sentiment", which were hard to predict in response to necessary, but painful reforms.
Romanians earn less than $100 in monthly wages and their purchasing power has been halved in the post-communist era.

Isarescu said price corrections and macro-stabilisation should coincide with a measure of social protection and resumed international financial support for reforms, which he said "should be explained to the population".
